newsitem.title: GERMANY: New German shop hours a disaster - retail union.
newsitem.headline: New German shop hours a disaster - retail union.

text.p: Germany's attempt to extend some of Europe's most consumer-unfriendly shopping hours is turning into a disaster, one of the country's main trade unions said on Tuesday.

Customer service levels have plummeted, smaller shops are seeing dangerous erosions of their business by larger stores, and laws governing maximum working hours are being flouted, officials of the HBV retail, banking and insurance union said.

The decision by many shops to try to cover longer working hours with their existing sales force has meant the experiment has done nothing to create new jobs in a country where unemployment is near all-time highs, it added.
"When you look at what was promised and what has actually happened, it is very disappointing," Doris Furbeth, HBV retail sector specialist told a news conference in Frankfurt.
Under the new hours introduced at the start of November, shops can stay open until 8.00 pm on weekdays and until 4.00 pm on a Saturday.
The German retailers association the HDE has agreed the experiment got off to a slow start, but a spokesman said earlier this week that late weekday sales were increasing.
While the German change of hours was significant, they are still way behind the virtually unregulated shopping hours in the United States and those that British retailers have pushed through.

Furbeth said that in the state of Hesse, home to many of the wealthy commuters employed in Frankfurt's banking industry, retail work councils were reporting no significant increase in sales or staff levels because of the longer hours.

"What you are seeing is that shops are sharing the extra hours among the same number of workers, while the smaller ones are having to get rid of staff because they are losing out to the big stores," she said.
She added that retail sector work contracts banning anything more than an 11-hour day were nonetheless being regularly flouted.

While welcomed by large retail groups and many younger consumers, the new opening hours have elsewhere been met with scepticism and outright hostility in an often conservative, family-centred country.

"For shop workers, housework is now often being left undone, they're too tired to have a conversation when they get home in the evening and they haven't even got a proper weekend left any more," Furbeth said.
HBV said it was possible that after the Christmas sales period German shops could retreat from opening so long unless they started seeing sizeable increases in sales.

Last weekend shoppers largely ignored specially-extended Saturday openings by many stores ahead of Christmas because, as retailers laters confessed, they were confused over what hours were applicable.
But some, such as the large Munich-based department store Karstadt, said the overall sales trend was higher.
